text: Teleportation used entanglement plus two classical bits to send one qubit's worth of quantum information. Superdense coding runs the idea in the opposite direction: using entanglement plus one physically transmitted qubit, Alice sends Bob two classical bits, double what a single qubit could carry on its own.

Alice and Bob start by sharing a Bell pair, Alice holding q1, Bob holding q2. To send one of four 2-bit messages, Alice applies a single gate to only her own qubit: identity for 00, X for 01, Z for 10, or X then Z for 11, then physically sends q1 to Bob. Verifying the 11 case directly: applying X to the Bell pair swaps two amplitudes, and the following Z flips the sign on whichever one now has q1 equal to 1 — exactly matching the table.

Bob decodes by running CNOT with q1 as control and q2 as target, then H on q1, then measuring both. Running that on the 11-encoded state: CNOT un-spreads the entanglement, and H collapses the result entirely onto the ket-11 component — Bob measures 1, 1 with probability 1. The same procedure applied to each of the other three encoded states returns exactly 00, 01, or 10, every time, with no ambiguity.

One physically transmitted qubit, combined with one pre-shared entangled pair, carries 2 classical bits — exactly double the usual 1-bit-per-qubit limit. That looks like it beats a fundamental law, but it doesn't: the Bell pair had to be created and distributed to both parties before Alice even knew her message, and that earlier step already cost one physical qubit transmission. Superdense coding front-loads that cost so the later, time-critical transmission can carry twice the information — no channel-capacity law is actually broken.
Next lesson addresses the obvious objection to both of these protocols directly: why neither one violates the no-cloning theorem or allows faster-than-light signaling.
